client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. I can't seem to focus at work at all — I'll be in the middle of a task and then just completely lose my train of thought, or I'll find myself staring at nothing for long stretches of time. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, because it's not like anything can change what happened.
therapist: I'm really sorry for the loss of your grandmother — grief can make it so hard to hold onto even the simplest things, and what you're describing makes complete sense. I notice that even as you're saying the words, there's something in your voice that sounds quite heavy and subdued, almost like you're carrying more than what you're letting yourself fully express right now. I wonder — when you say talking won't help because nothing can change, does part of you feel like your pain doesn't deserve space, or that allowing yourself to feel it fully might be too much to face?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Maybe both, I don't know. Like, I feel guilty even taking up space with this because she lived a long life and people kept telling me I should be grateful for the time we had — so somewhere along the way I think I started telling myself I don't really have the right to fall apart over it. But at the same time, yeah, the idea of actually sitting with how much I miss her feels like it could just swallow me whole.
therapist: What you're describing — this idea that your grief needs to be "earned" or justified — is such a painful and unfair burden to carry on top of the loss itself. There's no hierarchy for grief, and missing someone deeply isn't cancelled out by the fact that they lived a long life. I'm curious, when you imagine what it might actually feel like to give yourself full permission to grieve her, what comes up for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, when I try to imagine that, the first thing that comes up is just... a lot of fear. Like if I actually let myself go there, I won't be able to function at all — I'll break down at work or just stop being able to do the basic things I need to do to get through the day. I've been holding it together by keeping a kind of distance from it, and I'm not sure I trust that I'd be able to pull myself back together if I let that wall down.
therapist: That fear makes so much sense — you've built this wall because it's been protecting you, helping you keep showing up when you need to. What I want to gently offer is that grief doesn't usually work the way we fear it will; allowing yourself to feel it in small, supported doses tends to make it more manageable over time, not less. What do you think it would look like to take just a tiny step toward that grief — not tearing the wall down, but maybe finding a small window in it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and the "small window" idea sounds less terrifying than just... opening everything up at once. But I'm not even sure what that would look like practically — like, do I just sit in my apartment and think about her, and then what? I guess I'm worried that without knowing how to actually do it, I'll either avoid it completely or accidentally knock the whole wall down.
therapist: It sounds like even just talking through this possibility is stirring something up — there's a kind of urgency in how you're thinking about it, like you really want to get this right and not lose control. One practical "small window" might be setting a specific, time-limited intention — like giving yourself 10 minutes to look at a photo of her or write down one memory, and then gently returning to your day, so your mind learns that you can visit the grief and come back. Does something like that feel like it might be a manageable starting point, or does even that bring up the fear again?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: The 10-minute idea sounds manageable in theory, but I already know what's going to happen — I'll sit down with a photo and either feel nothing because I've gotten so good at shutting it out, or I'll feel everything and the 10 minutes will mean nothing because I won't be able to just stop and go back to my day like a switch I can flip. I guess I'm also a little alone in this, like there's no one around me who's really checking in or who I feel comfortable falling apart in front of, even for 10 minutes. That part makes the whole thing feel harder somehow.
therapist: The loneliness you just named feels really significant — like the grief itself is hard enough, but carrying it without anyone to witness it with you adds another layer of weight entirely. I also notice you're speaking with a kind of energy and speed right now, like there's a lot pressing up against that wall all at once, even as part of you is trying to think this through calmly. I'm wondering — is there even one person in your life, even someone unexpected, who might be more able to hold space for you than you're currently giving them credit for?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: There's maybe one person — my coworker Diane, who actually lost her mom a couple of years ago, so she'd probably understand more than most. But I haven't really let her in because I don't want to be a burden, and honestly I'm not sure I know how to even start that conversation without it feeling awkward or like I'm making a big deal out of something. It's easier to just say "I'm fine" when she asks how I'm doing and keep it surface level.
therapist: It's interesting that you know Diane would probably understand more than most, and yet "I'm fine" is still what comes out — there's something that feels safer about keeping that distance even with someone who's been through loss herself. That fear of being a burden is so common, and yet I wonder if it's actually protecting you or just keeping you more isolated in something you don't have to carry alone. What do you think Diane might actually feel if you gave her the chance to show up for you the way someone probably showed up for her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: When you put it that way, I think she'd probably actually want to be there for me — like maybe it would even mean something to her to be able to use what she went through to help someone else. But knowing that in my head and actually walking up to her and saying something real feels like two completely different things, and I'm already dreading the vulnerability of it, like what if I start crying in the middle of the office or she doesn't know what to say and it just becomes this weird uncomfortable thing between us.
therapist: You've actually just done something really important — you moved from "I don't know if she'd want that" to "she'd probably want to be there for me," and that's a meaningful shift. The vulnerability you're dreading is real, but it might help to know that the conversation doesn't have to be big or perfectly worded — even something as simple as "I've been having a hard time since my grandmother died and I remembered you went through something similar" opens the door without requiring you to fall apart. What feels like the smallest, most low-stakes version of that first sentence you could imagine actually saying to her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Maybe something like... "Hey, I've been struggling a bit lately, losing my grandmother hit me harder than I expected" — just keeping it that simple and seeing how she responds before deciding whether to say more. That feels slightly less terrifying than launching straight into the whole thing. But I'm still worried about the timing, like when do you even say something like that — do I just walk up to her desk out of nowhere, or wait for some natural moment that might never actually come and then I just keep putting it off forever?
therapist: That opening line you just came up with is genuinely good — it's honest, it's human, and it leaves room for the conversation to go at whatever pace feels right. On the timing question, I'd gently push back on waiting for the "perfect moment," because that can become its own form of avoidance — sometimes a quiet afternoon when things are slow and you catch her eye is moment enough. What would it mean to give yourself a small deadline, like sometime this week, so it stays a real intention rather than something that quietly slips away?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: A deadline this week feels both doable and like something I'll find a hundred reasons to talk myself out of the closer it gets. I know you're right that waiting for the perfect moment is probably just a dressed-up version of avoiding it, but there's still this part of me that worries if I force it before I feel ready, it'll come out wrong and then I'll have made things weird with the one person at work who might actually understand. I guess I'm asking — what if I try and it goes badly, and I end up feeling even more alone than I do now?
therapist: That "what if it goes badly" fear is worth taking seriously, but I'd invite you to also ask the other side of that question — what if it goes well, and you've been carrying this alone for a month when you didn't have to? The fact that your voice sounds soft and a little tentative right now, even as you're thinking this through, tells me this matters a lot to you, and that's exactly why it feels so risky. What's the smallest version of "it went badly" that you could imagine surviving — because I suspect you're more resilient than the fear is letting you believe right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess the smallest version of it going badly is just... it being a little awkward, Diane not really knowing what to say, and then we both go back to our desks and it's slightly weird for a day or two before things go back to normal. When I actually say it out loud like that, it doesn't sound like the end of the world. But I think what scares me more than the awkwardness is that I might open up even just a little and still feel just as alone afterward, like what if I take that risk and it still doesn't touch this feeling.
therapist: You just talked yourself through the "worst case" and found it survivable — that's actually a really significant moment, and I don't want it to slip past unnoticed. The deeper fear you're naming, that even reaching out might not touch the loneliness, makes sense after a month of holding this alone, but connection rarely dissolves grief in one conversation — it works more slowly, like light coming through that small window. What if the goal with Diane wasn't to feel completely un-alone afterward, but just to feel slightly less alone than you do right now — would that feel like enough to make it worth trying?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
